records.greek: Μετὰ ταῦτα ἦν ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων, καὶ ἀνέβη Ἰησοῦς εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα.
records.gloss: After these things was a feast of the Jews, and went up Jesus to Jerusalem.

L.1: After these things there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

R.1: Later on it was time for one of the Jewish festivals, so Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: a feast, without the article (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the feast, with the article (some important manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "the feast of the Jews". With the article the phrase would most naturally point to a well-known festival, either Passover or the Feast of Tabernacles. Without it, John leaves the festival unnamed. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: an unnamed festival; John does not say which
decisions.reason: Elsewhere John names the festivals: Passover (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), Tabernacles (7:2) and Dedication (10:22). Here he does not, and the story does not depend on which one it was. Many Jews went up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16), which is why there were crowds in the city (verse 13).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, whose festival it was
decisions.reason: As at 2:13, John names the festival as the people's, for readers who did not keep it. Jesus goes up to keep it as a Jew himself.

decisions.choice: went up: the usual way of speaking of travel to Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stands high in the hill country of Judea, and pilgrims always "went up" to it, whatever direction they came from (2:13; Psalm 122:4).

decisions.choice: a Jewish festival (B); one of the Jewish festivals (R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the Jewish people (meaning decision m3), so Balanced and Readable say "Jewish" without naming the leaders. "Festival" is the everyday word for a feast day of this kind.

decisions.choice: it was time for ... so
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that Jesus went to Jerusalem because of the festival, which the sentence implies.

records.heading: The healing at the pool

records.greek: ἔστιν δὲ ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ κολυμβήθρα ἡ ἐπιλεγομένη Ἑβραϊστὶ Βηθεσδά, πέντε στοὰς ἔχουσα·
records.gloss: There is now in the Jerusalem by the sheep [gate] a pool, the [one] being called in Hebrew Bethesda, five colonnades having;

L.2: Now there is in Jerusalem, by the Sheep [Gate], a pool which is called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porticoes.

R.2: In Jerusalem, near the gate called the Sheep Gate, there is a pool. In the Hebrew language it is called Bethesda. It has five porches with roofs.

decisions.choice: by the Sheep Gate there is a pool
alternatives: by the sheep pool there is a place called Bethesda
by the sheep market there is a pool
decisions.reason: The word for "sheep" is an adjective with no noun, so a noun has to be understood. Nehemiah names a Sheep Gate in the north wall of Jerusalem, near the temple (Nehemiah 3:1, 32; 12:39), and that is the most natural noun to supply. Some manuscripts have the word for "pool" in a different case, which would give "by the sheep pool", with Bethesda as the name of the place around it. The KJV's "sheep market" supplies a noun the text does not suggest.

decisions.choice: Bethesda (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts spell the name in several ways. Bethesda is found in many manuscripts of different kinds; Bethzatha in Codex Sinaiticus and a few others; Bethsaida in some early manuscripts, though that is the name of a town in Galilee (1:44). Bethzatha was also the name of a district just north of the temple, where the pool lay. A copper scroll found at Qumran appears to name a place with pools in Jerusalem by a form close to Bethesda. The evidence is evenly balanced; a footnote gives the other spellings. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: in Hebrew: in the language of the Jews of the land
decisions.reason: John uses this word for the local language of Judea (19:13, 17, 20; 20:16). In daily speech that was mostly Aramaic, a language close to Hebrew, and names such as this one could be either. The meaning of the name is uncertain; "house of mercy" and "house of the outpouring" have both been suggested.

decisions.choice: five porticoes: covered walkways with columns
decisions.reason: A portico is a roofed walkway open on one side, with a row of columns. Digging near the Church of St Anne in Jerusalem has uncovered two large pools side by side, separated by a wall of rock, which fits five porticoes: one on each of the four sides and one across the middle.

decisions.choice: there is: a present tense describing the place
decisions.reason: John says the pool "is" there. Writers often describe a place in the present, so the tense need not mean the pool was still standing when John wrote; it does show that he knew the place well.

decisions.choice: Sheep [Gate] (L); Sheep Gate (B, R)
decisions.reason: Every level supplies "Gate" (meaning decision m1); Literal shows it in brackets.

decisions.choice: porticoes (L, B); porches with roofs (R)
decisions.reason: "Portico" is the exact word for a roofed walkway with columns; Readable describes it in plain words.

decisions.choice: in Hebrew
decisions.reason: Keeps the word John used; meaning decision m3 explains which language this was.

records.greek: ἐν ταύταις κατέκειτο πλῆθος τῶν ἀσθενούντων, τυφλῶν, χωλῶν, ξηρῶν.
records.gloss: In these were lying a multitude of the being sick, blind, lame, withered.

L.3: In these lay a multitude of the sick, blind, lame, withered.

R.3: Lots of sick people would lie there in the porches. Some were blind, some could not walk well, and some had arms or legs they could not move.

decisions.choice: the verse ends here; the words about the angel stirring the water (verses 3b-4) are not part of the text
alternatives: "... withered, waiting for the moving of the water. For an angel went down at certain times into the pool and stirred the water; whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was made well of whatever disease he had."
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add that the sick were waiting for the water to move, and then explain why: from time to time an angel came down into the pool and stirred up the water, and the first person to get into the water after it was stirred was healed, whatever the disease. The oldest manuscripts, among them two early papyri, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have these words. Some manuscripts have only part of them, others mark them as doubtful, and the wording varies a good deal from copy to copy. They seem to have been added to explain the sick man's words in verse 7. The SBLGNT does not print them, so verse 4 is not in the text and the numbering passes from verse 3 to verse 5. A footnote gives the added words. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: withered: with limbs shrunken or paralyzed
decisions.reason: The word means dry or withered. Used of people, as of the man with the "withered" hand (Mark 3:1-3), it describes limbs that have wasted and cannot be used.

decisions.choice: lay: the imperfect describes what was usual there
alternatives: were lying there on that one day
decisions.reason: The tense pictures a lasting scene: the porticoes were a place where sick people regularly lay, hoping to be healed (verse 7).

decisions.choice: used to lie, paralyzed (B); would lie, arms or legs they could not move (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that this was the usual scene (meaning decision m3) and say in plain words what "withered" meant (m2).

records.greek: ἦν δέ τις ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖ τριάκοντα ὀκτὼ ἔτη ἔχων ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: Was now a certain man there thirty eight years having in the weakness of him;

L.5: Now a certain man was there who had been thirty-eight years in his illness.

R.5: One of the men lying there had been sick for thirty-eight years.

decisions.choice: having thirty-eight years in his illness: he had been ill for thirty-eight years
decisions.reason: To "have" a length of time in a state is a common way of saying how long it has lasted (compare verse 6, and 8:57; 11:17). The illness had lasted most of an ordinary lifetime. John does not name it, but verse 7 shows that he could not move quickly.

decisions.choice: thirty-eight years: a length of time, with no further meaning drawn from it
alternatives: an echo of the thirty-eight years Israel spent in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14)
decisions.reason: The number matches the years of Israel's wandering after the spies' report (Deuteronomy 2:14), and some readers see a picture of Israel in the man. John draws no such link, and the number fits a plain report of a long illness.

decisions.choice: One of the men lying there
decisions.reason: Readable ties the man to the sick people of verse 3.

records.greek: τοῦτον ἰδὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς κατακείμενον, καὶ γνοὺς ὅτι πολὺν ἤδη χρόνον ἔχει, λέγει αὐτῷ· Θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι;
records.gloss: This [one] having seen the Jesus lying, and having known that much already time he has, says to him, "Do you want well to become?"

L.6: When Jesus saw this [man] lying [there] and knew that he had already been [so] a long time, He says to him, "Do you want to become well?"

R.6: Jesus saw the man lying there. He knew that the man had been sick for a long time. So Jesus asked him, "Would you like to get well?"

decisions.choice: knew, having learned it; John does not say how
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to come to know as well as to know. Jesus may have been told, or seen it for himself; John shows him knowing what others have not told him elsewhere (1:47-48; 2:24-25; 4:17-18), but here he does not say which.

decisions.choice: Jesus takes the first step and asks the man what he wants
alternatives: a question that doubts the man's wish to be healed
decisions.reason: The man does not ask Jesus for anything; Jesus comes to him. The question is not idle: it draws the man's attention from the pool to the one speaking with him. His answer (verse 7) shows that he can think only of the water.

decisions.choice: well: whole, sound in body
decisions.reason: The word means healthy or whole. It runs through the story (verses 6, 9, 11, 14, 15) and is taken up again in 7:23, where Jesus speaks of having made "a whole man well" on the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: asked (B, R); also told (verse 8) and found (verse 14)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 6, 8 and 14).

decisions.choice: well
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the same word each time it comes in the story (meaning decision m3), so that the repeated word stays visible.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ ὁ ἀσθενῶν· Κύριε, ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω ἵνα ὅταν ταραχθῇ τὸ ὕδωρ βάλῃ με εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν· ἐν ᾧ δὲ ἔρχομαι ἐγὼ ἄλλος πρὸ ἐμοῦ καταβαίνει.
records.gloss: Answered him the being sick, "Sir, a man not I have that when is stirred the water he may put me into the pool; in which [time] but am coming I, another before me goes down."

L.7: The sick [man] answered Him, "Sir, I do not have a person to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up; but while I am coming, another goes down before me."

R.7: The sick man answered Him, "Sir, there is no one to help me get into the pool when the water starts to move. While I am trying to get there, someone else always gets in first."

decisions.choice: Sir: a polite address to a man he does not know
alternatives: Lord, a confession of who Jesus is
decisions.reason: The word is the one later used of Jesus as Lord (20:28), but it was also the ordinary courteous way to address a man. This man does not know who Jesus is (verse 13). A footnote gives "Lord".

decisions.choice: when the water is stirred: the sick believed that the first one into the water after it moved would be healed
alternatives: John himself teaches that the water healed
decisions.reason: The man speaks of a belief held by those who waited at the pool: from time to time the water was disturbed, perhaps by a spring or by water let in from another pool, and the first one in was thought to be healed. John reports what the man believed; he does not say whether it was so. The words added in some manuscripts after verse 3 explain the belief (see the note there).

decisions.choice: a man: anyone at all to help him
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for a person, and here it means he has no one at all. It also sets up the contrast of the story: the man who has no one to help him is found by Jesus.

decisions.choice: while I am coming, another goes down: what happens each time
decisions.reason: The present tenses describe what keeps happening: he is too slow, and every time someone else gets in first.

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: Shows the polite address (meaning decision m1); "Lord" would put in his mouth a confession he has not made.

decisions.choice: a {{gender:person|man}}
decisions.reason: The word means a person of either sex (meaning decision m3), so Literal gives the inclusive word by default and "man" as the alternative. Balanced and Readable say "no one", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: always
decisions.reason: Readable shows that this keeps happening (meaning decision m4).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἔγειρε ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ περιπάτει.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "Rise, take up the mat of you and walk."

L.8: Jesus says to him, "Rise, take up your mat, and walk."

R.8: Jesus told him, "Get up! Take your mat with you and walk!"

decisions.choice: mat: a poor person's light bedding that could be rolled up and carried
decisions.reason: The word is a common one for the thin mattress or pallet that poorer people slept on. It was light enough to carry, as the paralyzed man's mat is in Mark 2:4-12.

decisions.choice: two commands for single acts, then one for going on: get up, take up, and walk about
decisions.reason: The first two commands are for single acts. The third, "walk", is in a form that describes ongoing action: he is to start walking and keep on. Jesus heals by his word alone, as with the official's son (4:50).

decisions.choice: start walking
decisions.reason: Shows that the command is to begin walking and keep on (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: mat
decisions.reason: "Bed" suggests furniture too heavy to carry; "mat" gives the right picture (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: καὶ εὐθέως ἐγένετο ὑγιὴς ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἦρε τὸν κράβαττον αὐτοῦ καὶ περιεπάτει.
records.gloss: And immediately became well the man and took up the mat of him and was walking.

L.9: And immediately the man became well, and he took up his mat and was walking.

R.9: Right away the man was well! He picked up his mat and started walking.

decisions.choice: the healing is immediate and complete, and the man does exactly what Jesus said
decisions.reason: The narrative repeats the words of the command (verse 8): he took up his mat and walked. A man who could not reach the water in time now walks, at Jesus's word alone. John calls such deeds signs (2:11; 4:54); this one leads into Jesus's words about the Son giving life (5:21).

decisions.choice: was walking: began to walk about
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect, like the command in verse 8. It pictures him starting to walk and carrying on, which is how the authorities come to see him carrying the mat (verse 10).

decisions.choice: began walking about (B); started walking (R)
decisions.reason: Shows the beginning of an action that went on (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: Ἦν δὲ σάββατον ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: Was now Sabbath on that the day.

L.9: Now it was Sabbath on that day.

R.9: This happened on a Sabbath, the weekly day of rest.

decisions.choice: Sabbath: the seventh day, kept holy by resting from work
decisions.reason: God commanded Israel to do no work on the seventh day of the week, from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15). Keeping the Sabbath marked the Jews out among the nations, and it was guarded with great care.

decisions.choice: a late remark that turns the story
decisions.reason: John mentions the day only after the healing is over, as he does in 9:14. The remark turns a healing story into a dispute: everything that follows (verses 10-18) is about the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: And this happened on a Sabbath (B, R)
alternatives: Now that day was a Sabbath
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable tie the remark to the healing just told, which is the point of placing it here (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the weekly day of rest
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word for readers who do not know it (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἔλεγον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τῷ τεθεραπευμένῳ· Σάββατόν ἐστιν, καὶ οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἆραι τὸν κράβαττον.
records.gloss: Were saying therefore the Jews to the [one] having been healed, "Sabbath it is, and not it is lawful for you to take up the mat."

L.10: So the Jews were saying to the [man] who had been healed, "It is Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to carry the mat."

R.10: So the Jewish leaders spoke to the man who had been healed. "Today is the Sabbath!" they said. "The law does not allow you to carry your mat."

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: They speak with authority about what the Law allows, they question the man about who told him to break it (verse 12), and they go on to persecute Jesus and seek to kill him (verses 16, 18). That is the leadership, not the people as a whole: the healed man, the crowd and Jesus himself are all Jews.

decisions.choice: carrying a load on the Sabbath counted as work
decisions.reason: Through Jeremiah God forbade carrying a load out of one's house or through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-22), and Nehemiah stopped people bringing loads into the city on that day (Nehemiah 13:15-19). Later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah about AD 200, lists carrying a thing from one place to another among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Shabbat 7:2). By that rule, the man's mat was a load.

decisions.choice: were saying: they confronted him, perhaps more than once
decisions.reason: The verb is imperfect. It may simply set the scene of an exchange, or show them pressing the point.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: against the law (B); the law does not allow (R)
decisions.reason: Says plainly what "not lawful" means: forbidden by the Law as they understood it (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ὃς δὲ ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς· Ὁ ποιήσας με ὑγιῆ ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν Ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ περιπάτει.
records.gloss: He but answered them, "The [one] having made me well, that [one] to me said, 'Take up the mat of you and walk.'"

L.11: But he answered them, "The one who made me well, that [one] said to me, 'Take up your mat and walk.'"

R.11: He answered, "The man who made me well told me, 'Take your mat with you and walk.'"

decisions.choice: that one: he points to his healer as the one responsible
decisions.reason: The man puts "the one who made me well" first and then repeats him with an emphatic "that one". He defends himself by pointing to the authority of the one who healed him: someone who could do that had the right to tell him what to do.

decisions.choice: made me well: the phrase recurs as a mark of what Jesus has done
decisions.reason: "The one who made me well" comes again in verse 15, and Jesus uses the same words in 7:23. The authorities ask about the command to carry the mat (verse 12); the man keeps speaking of the healing.

decisions.choice: The man who
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plain word; the healed man does not yet know who Jesus is.

records.greek: ἠρώτησαν οὖν αὐτόν· Τίς ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ εἰπών σοι· Ἆρον καὶ περιπάτει;
records.gloss: They asked therefore him, "Who is the man the [one] having said to you, 'Take up and walk'?"

L.12: So they asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take [it] up and walk'?"

R.12: So they asked him, "Who is the man who told you to pick up your mat and walk?"

decisions.choice: they ask about the command, not the healing
decisions.reason: The man has spoken of the one who made him well; the authorities ask only who told him to carry his mat. Their concern is the breach of the Sabbath rule, not the healing.

decisions.choice: the man: an ordinary word, perhaps with a note of disdain
decisions.reason: "Man" is a plain word, but set against "the one who made me well" it may suggest they think of Jesus as just some fellow who told the man to break the Law.

decisions.choice: Take [it] up
decisions.reason: The Greek command has no object here; Literal supplies "it" in brackets.

records.greek: ὁ δὲ ἰαθεὶς οὐκ ᾔδει τίς ἐστιν, ὁ γὰρ Ἰησοῦς ἐξένευσεν ὄχλου ὄντος ἐν τῷ τόπῳ.
records.gloss: The [one] but having been healed not knew who it is, for the Jesus withdrew, a crowd being in the place.

L.13: But the one who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place.

R.13: But the man who had been healed did not know who had made him well. There were many people there, and Jesus had quietly left.

decisions.choice: withdrew: turned aside and slipped off
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn aside or withdraw. It is not used elsewhere in the New Testament, and it suggests leaving quietly rather than fleeing.

decisions.choice: a crowd being in the place: the crowd let Jesus leave unnoticed
alternatives: Jesus withdrew to avoid the crowd
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the circumstances of his leaving. Most naturally the crowd explains why the man lost sight of him; it may also suggest why Jesus left, to avoid attention. The two fit together, and neither changes what happened.

decisions.choice: the man did not know who Jesus was
decisions.reason: He had been healed without asking or believing first, and he did not even know his healer's name. Jesus finds him again in verse 14.

decisions.choice: moved off without being noticed (B); quietly left (R)
decisions.reason: Shows the sense of the verb and the part the crowd played (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

records.greek: μετὰ ταῦτα εὑρίσκει αὐτὸν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἴδε ὑγιὴς γέγονας· μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε, ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν σοί τι γένηται.
records.gloss: After these things finds him the Jesus in the temple and said to him, "See, well you have become; no longer sin, that not worse to you something may happen."

L.14: After these things Jesus finds him in the temple and said to him, "See, you have become well; sin no longer, so that something worse may not happen to you."

R.14: Later Jesus found the man in the temple courts. He said to him, "Look, you are well now. Do not go on sinning. If you do, something worse could happen to you."

decisions.choice: stop sinning, so that nothing worse happens: a warning, not a statement that sin caused the illness
alternatives: the man's illness was a punishment for a particular sin
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say that the man's illness was caused by sin. In 9:2-3 he rejects the idea that a man's blindness came from his own sin or his parents'. Yet Scripture also speaks of sin that brings sickness in some cases (1 Corinthians 11:29-30; James 5:15-16), so the warning may suggest a link here without saying what it was. "Something worse" than thirty-eight years of illness is left unnamed; in the words that follow, Jesus speaks of judgment (5:24, 29).

decisions.choice: no longer sin: stop and do not go on
decisions.reason: The command is in a form that describes ongoing action, with "no longer": the man is not to continue in sin. The same words are spoken to the woman in 8:11.

decisions.choice: Jesus finds him: it is Jesus who seeks out the man
decisions.reason: As in 1:43 and 9:35, Jesus is the one who finds. The man did not know who had healed him (verse 13); Jesus comes to him again.

decisions.choice: the temple: the temple courts
decisions.reason: The word is the one for the whole temple area with its courts, where people gathered, not the sanctuary itself.

decisions.choice: temple area (B); temple courts (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for this word in John (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: See (L); Look (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Behold" is no longer everyday speech; the word calls attention to what has happened to him.

records.greek: ἀπῆλθεν ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἀνήγγειλεν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὸν ὑγιῆ.
records.gloss: Went away the man and reported to the Jews that Jesus is the [one] having made him well.

L.15: The man went away and reported to the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.

R.15: The man went and told the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who had healed him.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the same authorities as in verses 10-13
decisions.reason: He goes back to those who had questioned him and answers their question of verse 12. The man himself is a Jew.

decisions.choice: reported: John does not say why the man told them
decisions.reason: The verb means to report or announce, and John uses it of making something known (4:25; 16:13-15). The man may have been clearing himself, or speaking up for his healer. John gives no motive, and the renderings give none.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: healed him
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plain word here; Literal and Balanced keep the phrase of verse 11.

records.greek: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐδίωκον οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὅτι ταῦτα ἐποίει ἐν σαββάτῳ.
records.gloss: And because of this were persecuting the Jews the Jesus, because these things he was doing on a Sabbath.

L.16: And because of this the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because He was doing these things on a Sabbath.

R.16: So the Jewish leaders began to go after Jesus, because He was doing things like this on the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities
decisions.reason: The same authorities as in verses 10-15, who now act against Jesus. It is not the people as a whole: Jesus, his disciples and the healed man are Jews.

decisions.choice: were persecuting: pursuing him as an offender
decisions.reason: The verb means to pursue, and so to harass or persecute. The imperfect shows an action begun and kept up. Verse 18 says what it led to: they wanted to kill him.

decisions.choice: these things he was doing: a habit, not one act
decisions.reason: The plural "these things" with an imperfect verb speaks of a practice. John tells of another Sabbath healing in chapter 9, and Jesus refers back to this one in 7:21-23.

decisions.choice: they persecuted Jesus (SBLGNT)
alternatives: "they persecuted Jesus and sought to kill him" (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "and they were seeking to kill him", as the King James Version reflects. The older manuscripts do not have it, and verse 18 says the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: began to persecute, kept doing (B); began to go after (R)
decisions.reason: Shows the beginning of an action that went on, and a habit of healing (meaning decisions m2 and m3); Readable uses plain words for "persecute".

records.greek: ὁ δὲ ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτοῖς· Ὁ πατήρ μου ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι.
records.gloss: He but answered them, "The Father of me until now is working, and I am working."

L.17: But He answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I also am working."

R.17: Jesus answered them, "My Father is still working, right up to today, and I am working too."

decisions.choice: God has never stopped working, on the Sabbath or any day
alternatives: God is working now, in this healing, only
decisions.reason: God rested on the seventh day from the work of creating (Genesis 2:2-3), yet he goes on giving life and upholding what he made (Psalm 104:27-30; 121:4). Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of Jesus's lifetime, likewise says that God never ceases to work (Allegorical Interpretation 1.5-6). "Until now" means up to this very moment. If God is at work on the Sabbath, then the Son's work of giving life is not a breach of it (5:19-21).

decisions.choice: my Father: Jesus speaks of God as his own Father
alternatives: our Father, as any Israelite might say
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say "our Father" but "my Father", as in 2:16, and sets his own work beside the Father's. Verse 18 shows that his hearers understood what this claimed.

decisions.choice: and I too am working: the same verb, the same tense
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the same verb for himself as for the Father. His work is the Father's work carried on (5:19).

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker, which the Greek leaves to the context.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} (L); My
decisions.reason: "My" at the start of the sentence is capitalized either way, so it is written plain.

records.greek: διὰ τοῦτο οὖν μᾶλλον ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἀποκτεῖναι ὅτι οὐ μόνον ἔλυε τὸ σάββατον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν θεόν, ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: Because of this therefore more were seeking him the Jews to kill, because not only he was loosing the Sabbath, but also Father own he was calling the God, equal himself making to the God.

L.18: Because of this, therefore, the Jews were seeking all the more to kill Him, because He not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also was calling God His own Father, making Himself equal to God.

R.18: Because of this the Jewish leaders tried even harder to find a way to kill Jesus. He was breaking the Sabbath, and more than that, He was calling God His own Father. That meant He was making Himself equal with God.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities
decisions.reason: The same authorities as in verses 10-16, now seeking his death (also 7:1, 19, 25). Not the people as a whole.

decisions.choice: breaking the Sabbath: treating it as not binding
decisions.reason: The verb means to loosen or undo, and so to break or set aside a law; John uses it so in 7:23 and 10:35. This was the charge as the authorities saw it. Jesus has answered it in verse 17, and answers it again in 7:21-23: his work is the Father's work.

decisions.choice: his own Father: claiming God as Father in a unique way
alternatives: Father in the sense any Israelite could use
decisions.reason: Israel could call God its Father (Isaiah 63:16; 64:8). The word "own" marks the difference: Jesus spoke of God as Father in a way that belonged to him alone, and set his work beside God's (verse 17).

decisions.choice: making himself equal to God: how the authorities understood his claim
alternatives: a claim Jesus made to be a second god
decisions.reason: John records their conclusion. He does not deny that Jesus is equal to God: the Word was God (1:1), and all are to honor the Son as they honor the Father (5:23). What the next verses deny is that the Son makes himself anything on his own: he does nothing of himself, but only what he sees the Father doing (5:19, 30). Compare Philippians 2:6.

decisions.choice: all the more: they were already set against him
decisions.reason: "All the more" looks back to verse 16: their hostility, already begun, grows into a settled wish to kill him. The imperfect shows them going on seeking it.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: two sentences (B: Besides ... ; R: He was ... and more than that ...)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the sentence and keep the build-up of "not only ... but also": the second charge is the graver one.

decisions.choice: That meant
decisions.reason: Readable spells out how the last phrase relates to the one before: calling God his own Father amounted to making himself equal with God (meaning decision m4).

records.greek: Ἀπεκρίνατο οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ οὐδὲν ἐὰν μή τι βλέπῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα· ἃ γὰρ ἂν ἐκεῖνος ποιῇ, ταῦτα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ.
records.gloss: Answered therefore the Jesus and was saying to them, "Truly truly I say to you, not is able the Son to do from himself nothing if not anything he may see the Father doing; what for ever that [one] may do, these things also the Son likewise does.

L.19: So Jesus answered and said to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, the Son is not able to do anything from Himself, except what He sees the Father doing; for whatever He does, these things the Son also does likewise.

R.19: Jesus answered them, "I tell you the truth: the Son cannot do anything just on His own. He does only what He sees the Father doing. Whatever the Father does, the Son does the same.

decisions.choice: Jesus answers the charge of 5:18
decisions.reason: The authorities wanted to kill Jesus because he called God his own Father, "making himself equal with God" (5:18). He does not take the claim back. He explains it: the Son's equality with the Father is not a rival claim to power but a complete unity of action, in which the Son does whatever the Father does (this verse) and receives the honor the Father receives (5:23).

decisions.choice: from himself: on his own, apart from the Father
alternatives: by his own power, as if the Son lacked ability
decisions.reason: The phrase ἀφ ἑαυτοῦ means acting on one's own initiative or authority, as in 7:17-18, 11:51, 14:10 and 16:13. The "cannot" describes the Son's relationship to the Father, not a lack of power: the Son never acts as a separate agent, because he and the Father act together (10:30; 14:10). Jesus says the same of himself in 5:30.

decisions.choice: whatever the Father does, the Son does the same works, in the same way
alternatives: the Son imitates the Father, doing similar things
decisions.reason: The pronoun ἐκεῖνος ("that one") refers to the Father. The sentence does not say the Son does similar things, but "these things", the very works the Father does, and "likewise". The next verses name two of them, giving life to the dead and judging (5:21-22), which in Scripture belong to God alone.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 5:24 and 5:25 as well.

decisions.choice: on his own
decisions.reason: Plain English for the idiom (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps "from himself", the Greek form. 5:30 uses the same wording.

decisions.choice: the Father
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the Father for the pronoun "that one", so the reader does not lose track of who is meant (meaning decision m3). Literal has "he".

decisions.choice: said (L); gave them this answer (B)
decisions.reason: "Answered and was saying" is a common way of introducing a reply; the second verb adds no separate action. Literal keeps both verbs and gives the second in the simple past.

records.heading: What the Son does

records.greek: ὁ γὰρ πατὴρ φιλεῖ τὸν υἱὸν καὶ πάντα δείκνυσιν αὐτῷ ἃ αὐτὸς ποιεῖ, καὶ μείζονα τούτων δείξει αὐτῷ ἔργα, ἵνα ὑμεῖς θαυμάζητε.
records.gloss: The for Father loves the Son and all things shows to him which he himself does, and greater than these he will show him works, so that you may marvel.

L.20: For the Father loves the Son and shows Him all things that He Himself does, and greater works than these He will show Him, so that you may marvel.

R.20: The Father loves the Son and shows Him everything He does. And He will show Him even greater works than these. Then you will be amazed.

decisions.choice: loves: the Father's love for the Son
alternatives: affection or friendship, a lesser love than the other verb
decisions.reason: φιλεῖ is one of John's two verbs for love. John uses both of the Father's love for the Son: 3:35 has the other verb, this verse has this one. Here, as there, the meaning is the same, so there is no difference in kind between the two (see the note at 21:15-17). The love is the reason the Father hides nothing from the Son.

decisions.choice: greater works: giving life to the dead and judging (5:21-29)
alternatives: only further and more striking signs, such as the raising of Lazarus
decisions.reason: "These" are works like the healing at the pool that started the dispute (5:1-9). The next sentences, which begin "for", say what is greater: raising the dead and giving them life, and carrying out judgment. The raising of Lazarus (11:43-44) is a sign of this greater work.

decisions.choice: so that you may marvel: astonishment, which is not yet belief
decisions.reason: The pronoun ὑμεῖς is stated, so it is emphatic: you, the very people who oppose him. Amazement at what Jesus does may lead to believing, or it may stop short of it; in 5:28 he tells them not to marvel, and in 7:21 the crowd marvels at one work and is still divided. Marveling is not the goal; believing is (5:24).

decisions.choice: astonished (B); amazed (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for marveling. Literal keeps "marvel". 5:28 uses the same words for the same verb.

decisions.choice: And there are greater works than these that he will show him
alternatives: And he will show him greater works than these
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the stress the Greek puts on "greater" by putting the works first.

records.greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐγείρει τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ ζῳοποιεῖ, οὕτως καὶ ὁ υἱὸς οὓς θέλει ζῳοποιεῖ.
records.gloss: Just as for the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son whom he wills gives life.

L.21: For just as the Father raises the dead and gives [them] life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills.

R.21: The Father raises people from the dead and gives them life. In the same way, the Son gives life to anyone He wants to.

decisions.choice: raising the dead and giving life is God's own work, and the Son does it
decisions.reason: In Scripture it is God who kills and makes alive, who brings down to the grave and raises up (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6); the king of Israel asks, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive?" (2 Kings 5:7). By saying the Son does the same, Jesus answers the charge that he makes himself equal with God (5:18).

decisions.choice: gives life: both raising to bodily life and giving eternal life now
alternatives: only the resurrection at the last day
decisions.reason: ζῳοποιεῖ means to make alive. The following verses use both senses: those who hear his word already have eternal life and have passed from death to life (5:24-25), and at the last day those in the tombs will come out (5:28-29).

decisions.choice: whom he wills: the Son gives life freely, and his will is one with the Father's
alternatives: the Son chooses independently of the Father
decisions.reason: The Son is not a tool that the Father uses; he gives life by his own choice. But his will is never separate from the Father's: he seeks only the will of the one who sent him (5:30), and the Father's will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him should have eternal life (6:40). The sentence does not say how the choice is made.

decisions.choice: [them] (L); them (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs an object for "gives life" after "raises the dead".

decisions.choice: chooses (B); wants to (R)
decisions.reason: "Wills" is formal; these words say the same thing in everyday English.

records.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ κρίνει οὐδένα, ἀλλὰ τὴν κρίσιν πᾶσαν δέδωκεν τῷ υἱῷ, ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν καθὼς τιμῶσι τὸν πατέρα.
records.gloss: Not even for the Father judges no one, but the judgment all he has given to the Son, \v 23 so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

L.22: For neither does the Father judge anyone, but He has given all judgment to the Son,
L.23: so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

R.22: The Father does not judge anyone. He has put all judging into the Son's hands,
R.23: so that everyone will honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

decisions.choice: the Father judges no one: he judges through the Son, not apart from him
alternatives: the Father has no part in judgment at all
decisions.reason: "For neither" ties this to 5:21: as the Son gives life, so also judging is in his hands. Scripture calls God the judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25), and Jesus later says that the Father "seeks and judges" (8:50). So the point is not that the Father has nothing to do with judgment, but that he carries it out through the Son.

decisions.choice: all judgment: the whole work of judging, deciding and passing sentence
decisions.reason: κρίσιν is the act and authority of judging, here without limit ("all"). The perfect δέδωκεν speaks of a gift already made and still in force. 5:27 says the same gift is "authority to carry out judgment".

decisions.choice: the Son receives the honor given to God
decisions.reason: "Just as" means the same honor, not a lesser one. In Isaiah 42:8 the LORD says he will not give his glory to another; yet the Father wills that the Son be honored as he is. This is the heart of Jesus's answer to 5:18.

decisions.choice: given the whole work of judging (B); put all judging into the Son's hands (R)
decisions.reason: Makes clear that "all judgment" is the task and right of judging, not a single verdict (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: everyone
decisions.reason: The Greek word means all people; "everyone" is already inclusive and needs no setting.

records.greek: ὁ μὴ τιμῶν τὸν υἱὸν οὐ τιμᾷ τὸν πατέρα τὸν πέμψαντα αὐτόν.
records.gloss: The [one] not honoring the Son not honors the Father the [one] having sent him.

L.23: The one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him.

R.23: Anyone who does not honor the Son is not honoring the Father either, because the Father is the one who sent Him.

decisions.choice: how an envoy is treated is how the sender is treated
decisions.reason: In the ancient world a messenger stood for the one who sent him. When the Ammonite king shamed David's envoys, David took it as done to himself (2 Samuel 10:1-5). Jesus says the same of his own messengers (13:20; Matthew 10:40). The Son is the Father's envoy, so dishonoring him dishonors the Father.

decisions.choice: the Father who sent him: the Son comes on the Father's mission
decisions.reason: "The one who sent me" is one of Jesus's commonest names for the Father in John (5:24, 30, 37; 6:38-39). It ties the Son's words and works to the Father's purpose.

decisions.choice: refuses honor ... refuses it
alternatives: does not honor ... does not honor (Literal)
decisions.reason: Keeps the repeated verb but makes the sentence run in Balanced.

decisions.choice: because the Father is the one who sent him
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the link that "who sent him" implies (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you that the [one] the word of me hearing and believing the [one] having sent me has life eternal, and into judgment not comes but has passed out of the death into the life.

L.24: Truly, truly I say to you, the one who hears My word and believes the one who sent Me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.

R.24: I tell you the truth: anyone who hears what I say and believes the one who sent Me already has eternal life. That person will not be judged guilty. They have left death behind and come into life.

decisions.choice: one person who both hears the Son's word and believes the Father
decisions.reason: One article governs both verbs: hearing and believing describe the same person. To believe "the one who sent me" is to trust the Father's testimony, which is heard in the Son's word (5:37-38; 12:44). Hearing here is hearing that takes the word in, as in 5:25 and 10:27.

decisions.choice: has eternal life: possessed now
alternatives: will have eternal life at the last day
decisions.reason: The verb is present: the one who believes has eternal life already, not only after death (3:36; 6:47). Eternal life is the life of the age to come, knowing the Father and the one he sent (17:3).

decisions.choice: judgment: condemnation, the verdict that goes against someone
alternatives: any judgment at all, so that believers are never examined
decisions.reason: Set against eternal life and passing from death to life, κρίσιν here is a judgment that condemns, as in 3:18-19 and "the resurrection of judgment" in 5:29. The sentence does not deny that all people stand before the Son as judge (5:22, 27); it says that for the one who believes, the outcome is not condemnation.

decisions.choice: has passed from death to life: a move already made, whose result stands
alternatives: will pass from death to life at the resurrection
decisions.reason: μεταβέβηκεν is perfect: the crossing has happened and its result remains. Death here is the state of being cut off from God's life, in which a person lives before believing; 1 John 3:14 uses the same words of believers. Bodily death still lies ahead (11:25), but it cannot undo this life.

decisions.choice: come under condemnation (B); be judged guilty (R)
decisions.reason: Gives the sense of judgment here (meaning decision m3), as in 3:17-18. Literal keeps "judgment" so the word family of 5:22-30 stays visible.

decisions.choice: already
decisions.reason: Brings out the present "has" and the perfect "has passed" (meaning decisions m2 and m4).

decisions.choice: {{gender:They have|He has}}
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence and needs a pronoun for anyone who believes; inclusive default. Literal and Balanced need none.

decisions.choice: what I say
decisions.reason: Plain words for "my word": the whole of Jesus's message.

records.greek: Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ νῦν ἐστιν ὅτε οἱ νεκροὶ ἀκούσουσιν τῆς φωνῆς τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ οἱ ἀκούσαντες ζήσουσιν.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you that is coming an hour and now is when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of the God and the [ones] having heard will live.

L.25: Truly, truly I say to you, an hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

R.25: I tell you the truth: a time is coming, and it has already started, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God. Those who listen to it will live.

decisions.choice: an hour is coming and now is: the time God has set for giving life, already begun in Jesus
decisions.reason: As at 4:23, the hour is still ahead and yet has already begun with Jesus present. This is not Jesus's own appointed hour, the hour of his death and glory (2:4; 12:23), but the time God has fixed for the dead to hear and live. 5:28 speaks of the same hour without "and now is".

decisions.choice: the dead: those who are spiritually dead, who hear the Son now and receive life
alternatives: the physically dead, raised during Jesus's ministry
the dead at the last day
decisions.reason: "And now is" puts this in the present, and 5:24 has just spoken of passing from death to life by hearing the Son's word. So the dead here are people without God's life, who come alive when they hear him (compare Ephesians 2:1, 5). Jesus's raising of the physically dead, such as Lazarus (11:43-44), is a sign of this. In 5:28-29 the bodily dead are meant.

decisions.choice: will hear ... those who hear: the voice reaches them; those who heed it live
decisions.reason: Not everyone who hears lives: the second "hear" means hearing that takes the voice in and responds, as the sheep hear the shepherd's voice (10:3, 27). In 5:28-29, by contrast, all in the tombs hear and come out, to life or to judgment.

decisions.choice: a time
decisions.reason: As at 4:21: "hour" sounds like sixty minutes. Literal and Balanced keep "hour" so John's thread of the hour stays visible.

decisions.choice: in fact it has already begun (B); it has already started (R)
decisions.reason: As at 4:23: plain words for the hour's present arrival (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Those who listen to it
decisions.reason: "Listen" brings out hearing that responds (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἔχει ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ, οὕτως καὶ τῷ υἱῷ ἔδωκεν ζωὴν ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ·
records.gloss: Just as for the Father has life in himself, so also to the Son he gave life to have in himself;

L.26: For just as the Father has life in Himself, so also He gave to the Son to have life in Himself.

R.26: The Father has life in Himself: His life does not come from anyone else. And He has given the Son that same life, so that the Son has it in Himself too.

decisions.choice: life in himself: life that is God's own, received from no one
decisions.reason: Everything that lives has received its life; God is the fountain of life (Psalm 36:10) and the living God (Jeremiah 10:10). "Just as ... so also" says the Son has the same life, not a lesser copy: "in him was life" (1:4). That is why the Son can give life to whom he wills (5:21).

decisions.choice: gave: the text does not say when, and leaves open whether this belongs to the Son's eternal relation to the Father or to his mission
alternatives: given to the Son only when he was sent into the world
describes only the Son's eternal relation to the Father
decisions.reason: The past tense ἔδωκεν states the gift without dating it. 1:4 says life was in the Word from the beginning, and 6:57 says the Son lives "because of the Father". The sentence teaches that the Son's life is both truly his own and received from the Father; it does not settle more than that.

decisions.choice: has given the Son life in himself
alternatives: has granted the Son also to have life in himself
decisions.reason: "Gave to the Son to have life in himself" is stiff in English; Balanced folds "to have" into "given ... life", which says the same.

decisions.choice: his life does not come from anyone else ... that same life
alternatives: has life in himself, and has given the Son to have life in himself
decisions.reason: Readable explains what "life in himself" means and that the Son's life is the same (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: has given
decisions.reason: The English perfect fits a gift whose effect continues; Literal keeps the simple past.

records.greek: καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ κρίσιν ποιεῖν, ὅτι υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστίν.
records.gloss: And authority he gave him judgment to do, because son of man he is.

L.27: And He gave Him authority to carry out judgment, because He is [the] Son of Man.

R.27: The Father has also given the Son the right to judge, because He is the Son of Man.

decisions.choice: Son of Man: the title, the figure of Daniel 7:13-14
alternatives: because he is a human being (son of man without the title)
decisions.reason: Only here in the Gospels is the phrase without articles: literally "because he is son of man". In Hebrew "son of man" can mean simply a human being (Psalm 8:5; Ezekiel 2:1), so this could mean that the one who judges people is himself human. But the sentence is about authority given to judge, which is what Daniel 7:13-14 describes: one like a son of man is given authority, glory and an everlasting kingdom. The Greek of Daniel 7:13 also lacks the articles (as do Revelation 1:13 and 14:14). Every level keeps the title; the footnote gives "because he is a human being".

decisions.choice: Daniel 7:13-14: authority given to the one like a son of man
decisions.reason: In Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days sits in judgment (Daniel 7:9-10), and one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given authority to rule over all peoples. Here the Father gives the Son authority to judge. The words for "authority" and "gave" match that scene.

decisions.choice: to do judgment: to carry out judgment, to act as judge
decisions.reason: κρίσιν ποιεῖν is an idiom for judging; the authority given is the authority of a judge (compare 5:22).

decisions.choice: [the] Son of Man
decisions.reason: The Greek has no articles (meaning decision m1); Literal shows that with brackets. Balanced and Readable write "the Son of Man", the book-wide title, capitalised.

decisions.choice: The Father ... the Son
decisions.reason: Readable names who gives and who receives, since the pronouns follow a long sentence.

decisions.choice: authority to pass judgment (B); the right to judge (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday wording for the idiom (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: μὴ θαυμάζετε τοῦτο, ὅτι ἔρχεται ὥρα ἐν ᾗ πάντες οἱ ἐν τοῖς μνημείοις ἀκούσουσιν τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκπορεύσονται οἱ τὰ ἀγαθὰ ποιήσαντες εἰς ἀνάστασιν ζωῆς, οἱ δὲ τὰ φαῦλα πράξαντες εἰς ἀνάστασιν κρίσεως.
records.gloss: Not marvel at this, because is coming an hour in which all those in the tombs will hear the voice of him \v 29 and will come out, those the good things having done to resurrection of life, those but the evil things having practiced to resurrection of judgment.

L.28: Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear His voice
L.29: and will come out, those who have done good things to a resurrection of life, but those who have practiced evil things to a resurrection of judgment.

R.28: Do not be amazed at this. A time is coming when all the dead in their graves will hear His voice
R.29: and come out. Those who have done good will rise from the dead and live. Those who have done evil will rise from the dead and be judged guilty.

decisions.choice: do not marvel at this: at what was just said, because of what is still to come
alternatives: do not marvel at this: that an hour is coming
decisions.reason: "This" points back to 5:25-27: that the Son gives life now and has authority to judge. The next clause gives the reason not to be amazed at it: something greater is coming. ὅτι can also introduce what "this" is ("do not marvel that an hour is coming"); the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: an hour is coming: the bodily resurrection at the last day
decisions.reason: Unlike 5:25 there is no "and now is". Those "in the tombs" are the bodily dead, and all of them hear and come out, not only those who heed. Elsewhere Jesus speaks of raising believers "on the last day" (6:39-40, 44, 54; compare 11:24). As in 5:25, the hour is the time God has set, not Jesus's own hour.

decisions.choice: Daniel 12:2: the dead rise, some to everlasting life and some to shame
decisions.reason: Daniel 12:2 says that many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace without end. Jesus takes up the same picture of two outcomes, and makes his own voice the one that wakes the dead.

decisions.choice: those who did good, those who practiced evil: deeds show how a person has responded to the Son
alternatives: life is earned by good deeds apart from believing
decisions.reason: This does not contradict 5:24, where life comes by hearing and believing. In 3:19-21 the same contrast appears: whoever practices φαῦλα hates the light, while whoever does the truth comes to the light. The work God asks is to believe in the one he sent (6:29). What people have done reveals whether they came to the light; it is not a separate way of earning life.

decisions.choice: judgment: condemnation
decisions.reason: Set against "resurrection of life", κρίσεως is the judgment that condemns, as in 5:24.

decisions.choice: A time
decisions.reason: As in 5:25. Literal and Balanced keep "hour".

decisions.choice: a resurrection that brings condemnation (B); rise from the dead and be judged guilty (R)
decisions.reason: Gives the sense of judgment here (meaning decision m5), as in 5:24.

decisions.choice: be astonished (B); be amazed (R)
decisions.reason: As in 5:20, which uses the same verb.

decisions.choice: all the dead in their graves
alternatives: all who are in the tombs
decisions.reason: Readable says who is in the tombs and uses the everyday word.

decisions.choice: done evil
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "practiced" to show that the Greek uses a different verb for the evil than for the good, as in 3:20-21; the difference is one of style, and Balanced and Readable use "done" for both.

records.greek: Οὐ δύναμαι ἐγὼ ποιεῖν ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐδέν· καθὼς ἀκούω κρίνω, καὶ ἡ κρίσις ἡ ἐμὴ δικαία ἐστίν, ὅτι οὐ ζητῶ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἐμὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πέμψαντός με.
records.gloss: Not am able I to do from myself nothing; just as I hear I judge, and the judgment the mine just is, because not I seek the will the mine but the will of the [one] having sent me.

L.30: I am not able to do anything from Myself. As I hear, I judge; and My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of the one who sent Me.

R.30: I cannot do anything just on My own. I judge the way the Father tells Me to, so My judging is right. I do not try to do what I want. I try to do what the one who sent Me wants.

decisions.choice: the Son of 5:19-29 is Jesus himself
decisions.reason: Jesus has spoken of "the Son" in the third person since 5:19; now he says "I", with the pronoun ἐγὼ stated for emphasis. The sentence repeats 5:19 ("from himself", "from myself") and closes the section.

decisions.choice: as I hear: as the Father tells him
alternatives: as he hears the evidence, like a human judge
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks and judges what he has heard from the Father (8:26, 28, 40; 12:49-50), just as he does what he sees the Father doing (5:19).

decisions.choice: his judgment is just because he seeks the will of the one who sent him
decisions.reason: A judge is fair when he has no interest of his own to serve. Jesus's food is to do the will of the one who sent him (4:34), and he came down from heaven for that purpose (6:38). So his judgment is God's own judgment.

decisions.choice: on my own
decisions.reason: As in 5:19. Literal keeps "from myself".

decisions.choice: the way the Father tells me to
decisions.reason: Readable says whom Jesus hears (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: what I want ... what the one who sent me wants
alternatives: my own will ... the will of the one who sent me
decisions.reason: Plain words for "will".

decisions.choice: right
decisions.reason: "Just" can mean "only" to young readers; "right" keeps the sense.

records.greek: Ἐὰν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής·
records.gloss: If I testify about myself, the testimony of me not is true;

L.31: If I am testifying about Myself, My testimony is not true.

R.31: If I am the only witness speaking about Myself, My testimony does not count as true.

decisions.choice: true: valid as evidence, able to stand in a court
alternatives: true as opposed to false, as if Jesus were admitting that he lies
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks in the terms of a court. The law of Moses lets a charge stand only on the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare 17:6; Numbers 35:30), so a person's word about himself, standing alone, does not settle a case. Jesus grants the rule and goes on to name the witnesses who stand with him. In 8:13-14 his opponents turn the rule against him, and he answers that his testimony is true even about himself, because he knows where he came from; there "true" means truthful, and he again names the Father as the second witness (8:17-18). The two sayings do not conflict: one is about what counts as evidence, the other about whether he speaks the truth.

decisions.choice: testify, testimony: the language of a trial, which runs through the rest of the chapter
decisions.reason: Jesus answers the charges of 5:16-18 as if in court, calling his witnesses one by one: John (5:33-35), the works the Father gave him (5:36), the Father himself (5:37) and the Scriptures (5:39); then he names Moses as the one who accuses his hearers (5:45). The verb and the noun for testifying occur eleven times in 5:31-39.

decisions.choice: testify ... testimony at every level
decisions.reason: The same pair of words for the verb and the noun throughout 5:31-39, as in 1:7 and 3:11, so the reader can follow the chain of witnesses. Readable uses "witness" only for the person who testifies.

decisions.choice: on my own behalf
decisions.reason: In a court, someone who testifies about himself speaks for his own case; Balanced says so plainly (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the only witness ... does not count as true
alternatives: If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the legal point (meaning decision m1), so that Jesus does not sound as if he were admitting to lying.

records.heading: Testimony about Jesus

records.greek: ἄλλος ἐστὶν ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ ἐμοῦ, καὶ οἶδα ὅτι ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία ἣν μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμοῦ.
records.gloss: Another is the [one] testifying about me, and I know that true is the testimony which he testifies about me.

L.32: Another is the one who testifies about Me, and I know that the testimony which He testifies about Me is true.

R.32: But there is another who testifies about Me: the Father. And I know that what He says about Me is true.

decisions.choice: another: the Father
decisions.reason: John is named in the next verse, and some have taken him to be the other witness. But Jesus goes on to say that he does not accept testimony from a human being (5:34), that he has testimony greater than John's (5:36), and that the Father who sent him has testified about him (5:37). In 8:18 he says it outright: the Father who sent him testifies about him. The present tense "testifies" and Jesus's "I know" fit the Father best.

decisions.choice: the second witness the law requires
decisions.reason: With the Father beside him, Jesus is not a lone witness, and the rule of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15) is met, as he says again in 8:17-18.

decisions.choice: But ... : the Father
alternatives: Another is the one who testifies about me
decisions.reason: Readable names the other witness (meaning decision m1) and adds "But" to mark the turn from verse 31.

decisions.choice: the testimony he gives
decisions.reason: Balanced avoids repeating the same root twice in one phrase.

records.greek: ὑμεῖς ἀπεστάλκατε πρὸς Ἰωάννην, καὶ μεμαρτύρηκε τῇ ἀληθείᾳ·
records.gloss: You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth;

L.33: You yourselves have sent [messengers] to John, and he has testified to the truth.

R.33: You sent messengers to ask John questions, and he testified to the truth.

decisions.choice: the delegation sent from Jerusalem to question John (1:19-28)
decisions.reason: The Jewish authorities in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask John who he was (1:19, 24). He told them he was not the Christ and pointed to the one coming after him (1:20, 26-27); the next day he called Jesus the Lamb of God (1:29). Jesus is speaking to the same authorities (5:16-18), and the pronoun "you" is emphatic: you yourselves asked for John's testimony.

decisions.choice: the truth: the truth about who Jesus is
decisions.reason: John's testimony was about Jesus (1:15, 29-34). The perfect tense "has testified" means that his testimony still stands, though John's own work is over (5:35).

decisions.choice: [messengers] (L); messengers (B); messengers to ask John questions (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the object of "sent" unstated; each level says who was sent (meaning decision m1), Literal in brackets.

decisions.choice: You yourselves
decisions.reason: Shows the emphatic pronoun (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἐγὼ δὲ οὐ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου τὴν μαρτυρίαν λαμβάνω, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λέγω ἵνα ὑμεῖς σωθῆτε.
records.gloss: But I not from a human the testimony receive, but these things I say so that you may be saved.

L.34: But I do not receive [my] testimony from a human being; rather, I say these things so that you may be saved.

R.34: I do not depend on testimony from people. I am telling you about John so that you can be saved.

decisions.choice: Jesus does not depend on human testimony; he mentions John for his hearers' sake
alternatives: Jesus rejects John's testimony as false
decisions.reason: John's testimony was true (5:33), but Jesus's claim does not rest on any human witness; the one who vouches for him is the Father (5:32, 37). The article ("the testimony") points to the testimony that counts for him. He reminds his hearers of John because they once welcomed John (5:35), and John's word could still lead them to him.

decisions.choice: be saved: rescued from judgment and given life
decisions.reason: As in 3:17, and in the terms of this chapter: the one who hears Jesus's word and believes the one who sent him has eternal life and does not come into judgment (5:24).

decisions.choice: [my]
decisions.reason: The Greek article points to the testimony Jesus relies on (meaning decision m1); Literal supplies "my" in brackets.

decisions.choice: accept (B); depend on (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means receive or accept. It recurs through the passage: Jesus does not accept glory from people (5:41), they do not accept him (5:43), and they accept glory from one another (5:44). Balanced says "accept" each time and Literal "receive" each time, so the thread stays visible.

decisions.choice: about John
decisions.reason: "These things" refers to what Jesus has just said about John's testimony; Readable says so.

decisions.choice: a human being (L, B); people (R), under the gender setting
decisions.reason: The word means any human being, not a male; the traditional "man" is the alternative, as in 2:25.

records.greek: ἐκεῖνος ἦν ὁ λύχνος ὁ καιόμενος καὶ φαίνων, ὑμεῖς δὲ ἠθελήσατε ἀγαλλιαθῆναι πρὸς ὥραν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: That one was the lamp the [one] burning and shining, and you were willing to rejoice for an hour in the light of him;

L.35: That one was the lamp that was burning and shining, and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light.

R.35: John was like a lamp that was lit and shining. For a short time you were happy to enjoy his light.

decisions.choice: a lamp, not the light
decisions.reason: John was not the light but came to testify about the light (1:8); Jesus is the light (1:9; 8:12). A lamp shines, but it has to be lit, and it burns down. The article may point to a familiar picture: in Psalm 132:17 God says he has prepared a lamp for his anointed one.

decisions.choice: was: John's work is over
decisions.reason: The past tense speaks of John's witness as finished. By this time he may have been put in prison or put to death; 3:24 notes that at an earlier point he had not yet been imprisoned.

decisions.choice: for an hour: for a short time
alternatives: for the length of an hour
decisions.reason: The phrase is an ordinary way of saying "for a while" (2 Corinthians 7:8; Galatians 2:5; Philemon 15). It is not the "hour" of Jesus's appointed time.

decisions.choice: you were willing to rejoice: their gladness in John was real but short-lived
decisions.reason: The verb for rejoicing means great gladness, even exultation. The people delighted in John for a while, but their delight did not carry them to the one he pointed to (5:33-34, 40).

decisions.choice: John
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "that one"; Balanced and Readable name John, so that no reader takes it to be Jesus.

decisions.choice: for a while (L); for a little while (B); for a short time (R)
decisions.reason: "For an hour" would sound like a clock time (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: like a lamp
decisions.reason: Readable makes the picture a comparison so that young readers do not take it literally.

records.greek: ἐγὼ δὲ ἔχω τὴν μαρτυρίαν μείζω τοῦ Ἰωάννου, τὰ γὰρ ἔργα ἃ δέδωκέν μοι ὁ πατὴρ ἵνα τελειώσω αὐτά, αὐτὰ τὰ ἔργα ἃ ποιῶ, μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμοῦ ὅτι ὁ πατήρ με ἀπέσταλκεν, καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ ἐκεῖνος μεμαρτύρηκεν περὶ ἐμοῦ.
records.gloss: But I have the testimony greater than of John; for the works which has given to me the Father so that I may complete them, the very works which I do, testify about me that the Father me has sent. \v 37 And the having-sent me Father, that one has testified about me.

L.36: But I have the testimony greater than John's; for the works that the Father has given Me so that I may complete them, the very works that I do, testify about Me that the Father has sent Me.
L.37: And the Father who sent Me, He has testified about Me.

R.36: But I have testimony that is greater than John's. The Father has given Me works to do and to finish. These works that I am doing testify about Me. They show that the Father has sent Me.
R.37: And the Father who sent Me has Himself testified about Me.

decisions.choice: the works: all that the Father has given Jesus to do, his signs included
decisions.reason: Where the narrator and the crowds speak of "signs", Jesus speaks of the "works" the Father has given him (5:20; 9:3-4; 10:25, 37-38; 14:10-11). They include the healing at the pool (5:17) and the greater works of giving life and judging (5:20-22). Because the Father is at work in them, they testify that he sent Jesus.

decisions.choice: complete: carry the Father's work through to its end
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 4:34 and 17:4; from the cross Jesus says "It is finished" (19:30), a word from the same root.

decisions.choice: the Father's testimony: left open, as the text leaves it
alternatives: what God told John about the Spirit coming down on Jesus (1:33)
decisions.reason: The perfect tense says that the Father has given his testimony and that it stands. Jesus does not say how. It may be the works through which the Father acts (5:36), the Scriptures that testify about Jesus (5:39), or the sign God gave John when the Spirit came down on Jesus (1:32-34). Verse 38 adds that his hearers do not receive it, because his word does not remain in them.

decisions.choice: he: emphatic, the Father himself
decisions.reason: The pronoun is not needed for the sense; it stresses the person: the Father himself, not a lesser witness.

decisions.choice: the works ... testify about me: they show that
alternatives: testify about me that the Father has sent me
decisions.reason: Balanced separates the testimony of the works from what it shows, so that the long Greek clause reads clearly.

decisions.choice: himself
decisions.reason: Shows the emphasis of meaning decision m4.

decisions.choice: The Father has given me works to do and to finish. These works ...
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the long sentence into short ones.

records.greek: οὔτε φωνὴν αὐτοῦ πώποτε ἀκηκόατε οὔτε εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἑωράκατε, καὶ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔχετε ἐν ὑμῖν μένοντα, ὅτι ὃν ἀπέστειλεν ἐκεῖνος τούτῳ ὑμεῖς οὐ πιστεύετε.
records.gloss: Neither voice of him ever have you heard nor form of him have you seen, \v 38 and the word of him not you have in you remaining, because whom sent that one, this one you not believe.

L.37: Neither have you ever heard His voice, nor have you seen His form,
L.38: and His word you do not have remaining in you, because the one whom He sent, Him you do not believe.

R.37: You have never heard His voice. You have never seen what He looks like.
R.38: And His word does not remain in you. That is clear, because you do not believe the one He sent.

decisions.choice: a contrast with Israel at Sinai
alternatives: a plain statement that no one has seen God (1:18)
decisions.reason: At Sinai Israel heard the voice of God out of the fire, though they saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12, 15, 33), and God said that Moses sees the form of the LORD (Numbers 12:8). Jesus's hearers claim that heritage, yet they have not heard God's voice: they do not recognize it in the one he sent. The words may instead restate that no one has ever seen God except the Son (1:18; 6:46), so that the Father's testimony reaches people only through him. Both readings lead to the point of verse 38.

decisions.choice: remain: stay and take root
decisions.reason: God's word has no lasting home in them. Jesus uses the same verb when he speaks of his words remaining in his disciples (15:7; compare 1 John 2:14).

decisions.choice: because: their unbelief shows that God's word is not in them
alternatives: their unbelief is the cause of God's word not remaining in them
decisions.reason: Unbelief here is the evidence: if God's word lived in them, they would recognize the one God sent.

decisions.choice: remain
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: "remain" in this sense, not the older "abide".

decisions.choice: the very one
decisions.reason: Shows the emphatic pronoun near the end of the Greek sentence.

decisions.choice: That is clear, because
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that their unbelief is the sign (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: Ἐραυνᾶτε τὰς γραφάς, ὅτι ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε ἐν αὐταῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔχειν· καὶ ἐκεῖναί εἰσιν αἱ μαρτυροῦσαι περὶ ἐμοῦ·
records.gloss: You search the Scriptures, because you think in them life eternal to have; and those are the [ones] testifying about me;

L.39: You search the Scriptures, because you think you have eternal life in them; and those are the [ones] testifying about Me.

R.39: You study the Scriptures carefully, because you think that in them you have eternal life, the life of the age to come. And the Scriptures themselves testify about Me.

decisions.choice: You search: a statement
decisions.reason: The Greek form can be either. Jesus goes on to give the reason they search ("because you think ...") and to say that they still will not come to him (5:40); both fit a statement about what they already do. As a command, the words would call them to search and find that the Scriptures point to him. A footnote gives the command.

decisions.choice: you think that in them you have eternal life: the Law as the way of life
decisions.reason: The Law itself promised life to those who keep it (Leviticus 18:5; Deuteronomy 30:15-20; 32:47). Jesus does not deny that the Scriptures speak of life; he says that they point to him, the one who gives it (5:21, 24-26).

decisions.choice: the Scriptures: the Jewish Scriptures, which Christians call the Old Testament
decisions.reason: The New Testament had not yet been written; Jesus means the Law, the Prophets and the other writings his hearers read.

decisions.choice: eternal life: the life of the age to come, God's own life, which begins now
decisions.reason: Key term, as in 3:15-16 and 5:24.

decisions.choice: pore over (B); study ... carefully (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to search or examine closely; Balanced and Readable use words that suggest close study of a text.

decisions.choice: the life of the age to come
decisions.reason: Readable explains eternal life once in the passage, as the book-wide choice for John allows (meaning decision m4).

records.greek: καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχητε.
records.gloss: and not you are willing to come to me so that life you may have.

L.40: And you are not willing to come to Me so that you may have life.

R.40: But you do not want to come to Me so that you can have that life.

decisions.choice: and: with the force of "and yet"
decisions.reason: The Scriptures testify about Jesus, and yet his hearers will not come to him. The plain "and" carries the contrast.

decisions.choice: not willing: they will not, not that they cannot
decisions.reason: The verb speaks of what someone wants or chooses. Jesus asked the man at the pool the same question with the same verb: "Do you want to be made well?" (5:6).

decisions.choice: come to me: put their trust in him
decisions.reason: In John, coming to Jesus and believing in him go together (6:35; 7:37-38).

decisions.choice: But ... do not want
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the contrast (meaning decision m1) and use the everyday verb.

records.greek: δόξαν παρὰ ἀνθρώπων οὐ λαμβάνω, ἀλλὰ ἔγνωκα ὑμᾶς ὅτι τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἔχετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.
records.gloss: Glory from humans not I receive, \v 42 but I have known you that the love of the God not you have in yourselves.

L.41: Glory from people I do not receive,
L.42: but I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.

R.41: I do not accept glory from people.
R.42: But I know you. In your hearts you do not love God.

decisions.choice: glory: honor and approval given by people
alternatives: the divine glory seen in Jesus (1:14)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the honor people give one another, a common sense of it. Jesus does not depend on human approval any more than on human testimony (5:34). The same contrast between glory from people and glory from God returns in 5:44, 7:18 and 12:43.

decisions.choice: the love of God: their love for God
alternatives: the love that comes from God
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean God's love or love for God. The context is about where their hearts are turned: they accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God (5:44). Israel's first command was to love the LORD with all the heart (Deuteronomy 6:5), and that love is what Jesus says is missing. The other senses are close: those who have God's love in them love him in return (1 John 4:19).

decisions.choice: I know you: Jesus knows their hearts
decisions.reason: The perfect tense means a settled knowledge. As in 2:24-25, Jesus knows what is in people; here he knows these hearers and says what is missing in them.

decisions.choice: love for God (B); you do not love God (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the phrase as it stands; Balanced and Readable give the sense chosen in meaning decision m2.

decisions.choice: Glory from people first
alternatives: I do not receive glory from people
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "glory" at the front, as the Greek does for emphasis.

decisions.choice: In your hearts
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday way of speaking about what is inside a person.

records.greek: ἐγὼ ἐλήλυθα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ πατρός μου καὶ οὐ λαμβάνετέ με· ἐὰν ἄλλος ἔλθῃ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῷ ἰδίῳ, ἐκεῖνον λήμψεσθε.
records.gloss: I have come in the name of the Father of me, and not you receive me; if another comes in the name the own, that one you will receive.

L.43: I have come in the name of My Father, and you do not receive Me; if another comes in his own name, that one you will receive.

R.43: I have come with My Father's authority, but you do not accept Me. If someone else comes on his own authority, you will accept him.

decisions.choice: in the name of: as his representative, with his authority
